guide.title: Campo Marzio, Rome: the Spanish Steps, piazza del Popolo, the Augustan monuments and the Pincio
guide.intro: Campo Marzio is R. IV, the fourth of Rome's rioni by toponymic code, and it fills the ground between the Tiber and the Pincian hill. The Spanish Steps climb out of piazza di Spagna to the church of Trinità dei Monti. Piazza del Popolo opens at the head of the Tridente, the three streets that fan south from it: via del Babuino, via del Corso and via di Ripetta. Two Augustan monuments stand in the rione, the Mausoleum of Augustus and the Ara Pacis, the altar now housed in a museum of its own. Above them the Pincio carries a public promenade laid out through the nineteenth century, with Villa Medici and the French Academy on its flank. Roma Capitale's boundary for the rione is a ring of named shopping streets, so several things a visitor files here belong to a neighbour.

sections.heading: The rione boundary
sections.body:
Roma Capitale states the rione's perimeter as a ring of named streets: piazzale Flaminio, via Luisa di Savoia, lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, lungotevere in Augusta, piazza del Porto di Ripetta, lungotevere Marzio, via del Cancello, via dei Portoghesi, via della Stelletta, piazza Campo Marzio, via degli Uffici del Vicario, via di Campo Marzio, piazza San Lorenzo in Lucina, via Frattina, piazza Mignanelli, via dei Due Macelli, via Capo le Case, via Francesco Crispi, via di Porta Pinciana and viale del Muro Torto. it.wikipedia's article on the rione gives the same ring as a list of neighbours: Quartiere Flaminio, Ludovisi, Colonna, Sant'Eustachio, Ponte and the Tiber. Via del Corso, via Frattina, via Sistina, via di Campo Marzio and piazza del Parlamento are named in that ring as boundaries, and a street named as a boundary is evidence of a line, not of what stands on either side of it.

Piazza San Lorenzo in Lucina carries two churches in two rioni. The basilica that gives the square its name stands in rione Colonna; the Rome Baptist Church at number 35 stands in Campo Marzio. Piazza di Spagna divides the same way in reverse: the square is Campo Marzio's, but Palazzo di Propaganda Fide, which fronts it, stands in rione Colonna and is a Lateran Treaty extraterritorial property. Palazzo Montecitorio, on piazza del Parlamento, is Colonna's too. On via del Corso the addresses are Campo Marzio's while the carriageway is shared with three other rioni: Casa di Goethe at 18, Gesù e Maria at 45, San Giacomo in Augusta at 499, the Grand Hotel Plaza at 126 and the Accademia di Belle Arti's succursale at 476 all stand inside the rione.

The Pincio, the Casina Valadier, the water clock, the busts and the Belvedere all stand in Campo Marzio, and several sources describe them as being in Villa Borghese. Villa Borghese is the name of a park, not of an administrative unit. The streets that lie wholly inside Campo Marzio include via Margutta, via della Croce, via Vittoria, via delle Carrozze, via Belsiana, via dei Greci, via del Vantaggio and via di San Sebastianello.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
it.wikipedia's article on the rione names Metro line A, with the Spagna and Flaminio stations, as the service reaching it. No source states more about either station, and neither walking times nor distances are given. Steer by addresses instead.

The northern end of the rione is piazza del Popolo, entered from piazzale Flaminio through the Porta del Popolo; the basilica of Santa Maria del Popolo is at Piazza del Popolo 12 and Santa Maria in Montesanto at 18. At the other end of via del Babuino is piazza di Spagna, where the Keats-Shelley Memorial House is at number 26, the Casa Museo Giorgio de Chirico at 31 and Babingtons at 23. Villa Medici is at Viale della Trinità dei Monti 1. The Augustan monuments are together on piazza Augusto Imperatore, with San Rocco all'Augusteo and Il Vero Alfredo at number 30 on the same square, and San Girolamo dei Croati on via di Ripetta.

Four more addresses cover the rest. Casa di Goethe is at Via del Corso 18; the Museo Atelier Canova-Tadolini at Via del Babuino 150/a, at the corner of via dei Greci; the Accademia di Belle Arti at Via di Ripetta 222, with its succursale at Via del Corso 476; and the Antico Caffè Greco at Via dei Condotti 86. Ponte Cavour crosses the Tiber from the rione; the bridge lies in two rioni, Campo Marzio and Prati, and Prati's guide covers the far bank.

sections.heading: Tickets and opening hours
sections.body:
Roma Capitale gives the Museo dell'Ara Pacis as open daily 9.30 to 19.30, with 9.30 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December and last admission one hour before closing. It gives Villa Medici as open 9.30 to 19.00, last admission 18.30, closed Tuesday. Casa di Goethe opens Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00, closed Monday, with last admission half an hour before closing. The Casa Museo Giorgio de Chirico admits visitors on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and the last Sunday of the month, closed Wednesday, with visits guided and a maximum of fifteen people per slot; tickets are 8 euro full and 5 euro reduced for under-18s and over-65s, free under 12, and are paid at the house on the day of the visit.

For eating and drinking the published times are Babingtons, Monday to Sunday 10.00 to 21.15, on piazza di Spagna; Il Vero Alfredo, Tuesday to Sunday 12.30 to 15.30 and 19.30 to 23.30, closed Monday lunchtime; and the Museo Atelier Canova-Tadolini, whose own site gives the bar and caffetteria daily 08.00 to 24.00 and the restaurant daily 12.00 to 23.00. The Accademia di Belle Arti's own contacts page gives its historic seat as open 07.30 to 19.15, Monday to Saturday. All Saints' on via del Babuino publishes its services rather than visiting hours: Sundays Low Mass at 8.30 and Sung Mass with choir at 10.30, Thursdays midweek Mass at 12.45, with worship in English.

Two of the rione's headline places cannot be walked into. The Mausoleum of Augustus has been closed since 6 June 2022 while work on piazza Augusto Imperatore goes forward. it.wikipedia records that the Antico Caffè Greco was temporarily closed during 2025 by the Ospedale Israelitico di Roma and that a reopening was reported in May 2026, and the business's own site currently carries a campaign about the future of the premises. And for two places that are open, no source states their opening hours, so none are given here: the Keats-Shelley Memorial House and the basilica of Santa Maria del Popolo.

faq.question: Are the Spanish Steps in Campo Marzio, and who built them?
faq.answer: Yes. The Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti, piazza di Spagna at its foot and the church of Trinità dei Monti at its head are all in Campo Marzio. Roma Capitale's Sovrintendenza dates the stair 1723 to 1726 and gives the design to the Roman architect Francesco De Sanctis, 1693 to 1740. The idea of a stair here is documented as early as 1559; a bequest by the Frenchman Stefano Gueffier in 1660 produced the first designs, Clement XI held a competition in 1717, and the work was finished under Benedict XIII in 1726. It was restored in 1995, restored again from October 2015, reopened on 22 September 2016 and walkable again from 23 September 2016.

faq.question: Can you go inside the Mausoleum of Augustus?
faq.answer: Not at present. Roma Capitale states that the mausoleum has been closed since 6 June 2022 while work on piazza Augusto Imperatore goes forward; a second phase of work began in 2025 and completion is stated as the end of 2026. You can still walk the square around it, and the Ara Pacis, the other surviving member of the same Augustan group, is open in its museum daily from 9.30 to 19.30.

faq.question: Is the Pincio part of Villa Borghese?
faq.answer: Villa Borghese is a park name, not the name of an administrative unit, and several sources use it loosely for the whole hilltop. The Pincio promenade, the Belvedere terrace at piazzale Napoleone I, the Casina Valadier, the water clock, the 229 busts and the Antinous obelisk all stand in rione Campo Marzio. The Galleria Borghese, by contrast, is outside the rione, in Q. III Pinciano.

faq.question: Which of the buildings here belong to other states?
faq.answer: None of them is Vatican City and none is in another country. Via dei Condotti 68 is the principal seat of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta; the Order has owned the building since 1630, and since 1834 it has been the residence of the Grand Master and the seat of the Order's government. Palazzo di Spagna houses the Embassy of Spain to the Holy See, and piazza di Spagna takes its name from it. Palazzo di Propaganda Fide, which fronts the same square, is a Lateran Treaty extraterritorial property standing in rione Colonna.

faq.question: What can you actually see from the Pincio terrace?
faq.answer: Roma Capitale enumerates the sightlines from piazzale Napoleone I: piazza del Popolo below, the dome of St Peter's on the horizon, Monte Mario to the right, the Quirinale to the left and the equestrian monument to Garibaldi on the Janiculum in the distance. The terrace sits on a three-arched loggia, the third of the three prospettive that carry the monumental access up from the square, and a nymphaeum was built into it in 1936 to a design by Raffaele De Vico as a mostra of the Acqua Vergine.

faq.question: Which church stands on piazza San Lorenzo in Lucina?
faq.answer: Two do, and they are in different rioni. The basilica of San Lorenzo in Lucina stands in rione Colonna. The Rome Baptist Church, an English-language Protestant congregation at number 35 on the same square, stands in rione Campo Marzio, which is both what the geometry gives and what it.wikipedia states.

photos.title: Piazza del Popolo and the Obelisco Flaminio
photos.description: Piazza del Popolo seen across the square, with the Obelisco Flaminio on Valadier's lion-fountain base, the basilica of Santa Maria del Popolo and its bell tower at the left, and the eastern hemicycle and the ramps up to the Pincio at the right.
photos.author: Diego Delso

places.name: Ara Pacis Augustae
places.summary: The altar of Augustan peace, voted by the Senate in 13 BC and inaugurated in 9 BC to mark Augustus' return from Gaul and Spain. This record is the altar; the museum built around it is written separately.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the altar was built along the via Flaminia at the edge of the northern Campo Marzio, and that the alluvial ground and the Tiber floods silted it over until it was buried and its position forgotten. Reconstruction was decided for the 1937 to 1938 bimillenary of Augustus' birth and entrusted to the archaeologist Giuseppe Moretti; it was physically carried out in the summer of 1938 inside a pavilion on via di Ripetta designed by Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo. it.wikipedia records that the original site stood one Roman mile, 1,472 m, from the pomerium.

places.name: Museo dell'Ara Pacis
places.summary: The civic museum that encloses the Ara Pacis, on the Tiber front of the rione. Roma Capitale gives the hours as open daily 9.30 to 19.30; on 24 and 31 December 9.30 to 14.00; last admission one hour before closing.
places.history: The building was designed by Richard Meier & Partners Architects and replaced the 1938 pavilion by Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo in which the altar had been reassembled. The text of the bronze Res Gestae tablets from the Mausoleum of Augustus is transcribed on the museum's wall.

places.name: Mausoleo di Augusto
places.summary: The circular dynastic tomb Octavian began in 28 BC on his return from Egypt, in what was then the unurbanised northern Campo Marzio. Roma Capitale gives its diameter as 300 Roman feet, about 87 m. Closed since 6 June 2022 while work on piazza Augusto Imperatore goes forward; a second phase of work began in 2025 and completion is stated as the end of 2026.
places.history: Roma Capitale records the ashes of Octavia, Marcellus, Agrippa, Drusus, Germanicus, Livia, Tiberius, Agrippina, Caligula, Britannicus, Claudius and Poppaea as deposited here, and that Nero and Julia the Elder were excluded. The mausoleum held the ashes of Vespasian and then of Nerva for a short time, and more than a century after the last deposition it was opened again for those of Julia Domna, wife of Septimius Severus. Two granite obelisks stood in front of it and were later reused, one set at piazza dell'Esquilino behind Santa Maria Maggiore in 1587 and the other in the fountain of the Dioscuri at piazza del Quirinale in 1783. The building served afterwards as a fortress, a garden, an amphitheatre and, in the early 1900s, a concert hall, and was restored between 1936 and 1938 with the demolition of the quarter around it. Roma Capitale names Rem Koolhaas as designer of the forthcoming museum layout and Bvlgari as its funder.

places.name: Porta del Popolo
places.summary: The gate between piazzale Flaminio and piazza del Popolo. Roma Capitale dates it to Aurelian, in the third century, and records that it was also called Porta Flaminia because the via Flaminia left the city through it and still does.
places.history: The outer face was commissioned by Pius IV from Michelangelo, who passed the work to Nanni di Baccio Bigio; it was executed between 1562 and 1565 on the model of the Arch of Titus, and its four columns came from the old St Peter's. The statues of Peter and Paul are by Francesco Mochi, 1638. The inner face is by Gian Lorenzo Bernini, made for Alexander VII for the arrival of Christina of Sweden on 23 December 1655, an event recorded by the inscription Felici faustoque ingressui MDCLV. it.wikipedia notes that the service door still carries the older spelling Campo Marzo, which was the rione's name until the Napoleonic period.

places.name: Obelisco Flaminio
places.summary: The Egyptian obelisk at the centre of piazza del Popolo, carved about 1300 BC for the temple of the Sun at Heliopolis, with hieroglyphs ordered by Seti I and Ramesses II. Roma Capitale gives it as 25.90 m tall, or 36.50 m with base and cross.
places.history: In 10 BC it was set on the spina of the Circus Maximus, together with the Obelisco Campense, to mark Octavian Augustus' conquest of Egypt. Three centuries later the Obelisco Lateranense followed. It was re-erected in piazza del Popolo in 1589 under Sixtus V, and in 1823 Leone XII had Valadier give it the raised base with the lion fountains that carries it now. The Obelisco Campense stands today in Colonna as the Obelisco di Montecitorio, and the Obelisco Lateranense in Monti.

places.name: Obelisco Sallustiano
places.address: Piazza della Trinità dei Monti, Roma RM
places.summary: The obelisk in piazza della Trinità dei Monti, standing in front of the church at the top of the stair that comes up from piazza di Spagna. it.wikipedia places it in rione Campo Marzio.
places.history: It is named Sallustiano for the Horti Sallustiani it came from, not for rione Sallustiano, which is a different unit of the city and does not hold it. it.wikipedia records that Sixtus V's new strada Felice, today via Sistina, was framed between two obelisks, the Esquiline one and this one.

places.name: Obelisco del Pincio (Obelisco di Antinoo)
places.summary: The obelisk on the Pincio, on the avenue that takes its name from it.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the emperor Hadrian dedicated the obelisk to his favourite Antinous, that it was found in the area of Porta Maggiore, and that it was moved and set up on the Pincio in 1822 at the wish of Pius VII.

places.name: Muro Torto
places.summary: A stretch of ancient substructure wall behind the Pincio, which gives viale del Muro Torto its name. Roma Capitale lists viale del Muro Torto among the streets that form the rione's edge.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes the Muro Torto as an ancient substructure wall of Rome that gives its name to the road running below the Pincio.

places.name: Porto di Ripetta
places.summary: A lost place with a surviving fountain. it.wikipedia describes the Porto di Ripetta as a river landing on the Tiber in the area in front of the church of San Girolamo dei Croati. The landing was demolished at the end of the nineteenth century; the fountain that served it remains.
places.history: Roma Capitale's Sovrintendenza names the port alongside the Spanish Steps and the Trevi Fountain as urban works of the same century. it.wikipedia's history of the rione records that the site of the port was later covered by Ponte Cavour, built in 1902 downstream of it.

places.name: Piazza di Spagna
places.summary: The square from which the Spanish Steps climb, with the Fontana della Barcaccia in it and the Colonna dell'Immacolata on piazza Mignanelli. Seen from above, it.wikipedia describes it as two triangles meeting at a point, in the shape of a butterfly's wings.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the square was already commercially important in the fifteenth century, for the number of inns and of houses lived in by foreigners, drawn here by the Spanish and French government missions. it.wikipedia records that the square takes its name from the Palazzo di Spagna, seat of the Spanish embassy to the Holy See from 1622. Palazzo di Propaganda Fide fronts the square but stands in rione Colonna.

places.name: Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti (the Spanish Steps)
places.summary: The stair that climbs from piazza di Spagna to the church of Trinità dei Monti. Roma Capitale's Sovrintendenza dates it 1723 to 1726 and gives the design to the Roman architect Francesco De Sanctis, 1693 to 1740.
places.history: The idea of a stair on this slope is documented as early as 1559, and twenty years later the Camera Apostolica bought the land. In 1660 the bequest of the Frenchman Stefano Gueffier produced the first designs, among them one attributed to Bernini's workshop that proposed the concave and convex walls and the pincer ramps. A dispute between the Papal State and the French crown over ownership of the ground delayed the work; Clement XI held a competition in 1717, building began under Innocent XIII, whose Conti eagles appear with the French fleurs-de-lis on the cippi, and it was finished under Benedict XIII in 1726. The Sovrintendenza records a full restoration in 1995, a further restoration from October 2015, a reopening on 22 September 2016 and the stair walkable again from 23 September 2016.

places.name: Fontana della Barcaccia
places.summary: The boat-shaped fountain in piazza di Spagna, built 1626 to 1629. Roma Capitale attributes it to Pietro Bernini, father of Gian Lorenzo; it.wikipedia gives it to Pietro Bernini and his son.
places.history: The boat has an identical bow and stern in an oval basin, and gunwales low enough that it reads as sinking. Two large coats of arms of Urban VIII, with three bees, are set on the outside of bow and stern, with water issuing from mock gunports at their sides. Roma Capitale connects the name with the boats used on the Tiber at the port of Ripetta, and its Sovrintendenza also records the naumachia tradition and the Tiber floods that carried boats up to the foot of Trinità dei Monti as rival explanations.

places.name: Colonna dell'Immacolata
places.summary: The marble column carrying a bronze Virgin on piazza Mignanelli. Roma Capitale gives the inauguration as 8 December 1857.
places.history: The cipollino shaft was found in 1777 in the convent of the Benedictines of Santa Maria in Campo Marzio; it was unfinished, and had probably never been used. It lay by Palazzo Montecitorio for about eighty years until 1854, when Pius IX decided to raise a monument after promulgating the dogma. Ferdinand II of the Two Sicilies funded it as a gesture of reconciliation after the lapse of the Chinea tribute, and the architect was Luigi Poletti. The column is about 12 m high and nearly 1.5 m in diameter, with four reliefs on the base and statues of Moses, Isaiah, Ezekiel and David at the corners; the bronze Virgin, 4 m high, is by Giuseppe Obici. Roma Capitale records that 220 firemen raised it, which is why the Vigili del Fuoco lay a wreath here every 8 December.

places.name: Keats-Shelley Memorial House
places.summary: The house on piazza di Spagna where John Keats died in 1821, first opened to the public in 1909 as a museum to Keats, Shelley and Byron, all three of whom lived in the district. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the eighteenth-century building still looks much as it did when Keats arrived in Rome, and that the museum holds letters, manuscripts, portraits and relics. It has two terraces, a bookshop and a screening room.

places.name: Casa Museo Giorgio de Chirico
places.summary: The three-floor apartment and studio on piazza di Spagna where Giorgio de Chirico lived and worked, kept as he left it and open on guided visits. The Fondazione gives the days as Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and the last Sunday of the month, closed Wednesday, with visits guided and a maximum of fifteen people per slot; tickets are 8 euro full and 5 euro reduced for under-18s and over-65s, free under 12, paid at the house on the day of the visit.
places.history: The Fondazione's own account records that de Chirico settled here in 1948, at the age of sixty, and spent the last thirty years of his life in the apartment.

places.name: Babingtons
places.summary: A tea room on piazza di Spagna. Roma Capitale lists it among the city's historic shops and gives the opening as Monday to Sunday, 10.00 to 21.15.
places.history: Roma Capitale records the founding in 1893 by Anna Maria Babington and Isabel Cargill, and that the business is run today by Isabel's great-grandchildren, Chiara and Rory.

places.name: Palazzo di Spagna
places.summary: Palazzo di Spagna houses the Embassy of Spain to the Holy See, and piazza di Spagna takes its name from it.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the square took its name from the palace in the seventeenth century, that the building extends onto via Borgognona and via Mario de' Fiori, and that the site covers 3,589 m² with 11,000 m² of building, plantings and terraces.

places.name: Palazzo Magistrale
places.summary: Via dei Condotti 68 is the principal seat of the Sovereign Military Order of Malta. The Order has owned the building since 1630, and since 1834 it has been the residence of the Grand Master and the seat of the Order's government.
places.history: The building stands on Italian soil in rione Campo Marzio, on the street that runs from via del Corso up to piazza di Spagna.

places.name: Piazza del Popolo
places.summary: The oval square entered through the Porta del Popolo and holding the Flaminio obelisk at its centre. Roma Capitale describes it as the point where via del Babuino, via di Ripetta and via del Corso meet.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates the urbanisation of the square from the second half of the sixteenth century, with a first fountain by Giacomo Della Porta, today in piazza Nicosia, and the obelisk raised in 1589. The Sovrintendenza gives the fuller sequence: the first fountain in 1572 by Della Porta, architect of the Roman people; the obelisk in 1589 under Sixtus V; the gate transformed by Bernini and the twin churches built through the 1600s; and the redesign of the whole square begun by Giuseppe Valadier in 1811, continued with the French architect L. M. Berthault in the Napoleonic years and finished in 1828, producing a great ellipse centred on the obelisk and closed by two hemicycles. It was restored and pedestrianised in 1997 and 1998.

places.name: Fontana dei Leoni in piazza del Popolo
places.summary: The fountain that surrounds the obelisk at the centre of the square: four round travertine basins at the corners of the stepped base, each with a white marble Egyptian-style lion on a stepped truncated pyramid.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza gives the work to Giuseppe Valadier, 1762 to 1839, and dates it 1814 to 1828, in marble and travertine, originally fed by the acquedotto Vergine. It replaced the sixteenth-century fountain that had stood in the square, which was dismantled and later re-erected in piazza Nicosia. The Sovrintendenza records maintenance work in 2015.

places.name: Fontana del Nettuno in piazza del Popolo
places.summary: The fountain set into the western hemicycle of piazza del Popolo: a semicircular travertine basin under a great travertine shell, with Neptune holding a trident and two tritons on dolphins at his feet.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza gives it as completed in 1823, by Valadier with Giovanni Ceccarini, about 1790 to 1861. Valadier's original scheme included two small ground-level lakes at the foot of the hemicycles, which were never built. Rome has a second and much older Fontana del Nettuno in piazza Navona, in rione Parione; this is the piazza del Popolo one.

places.name: Fontana della Dea Roma in piazza del Popolo
places.summary: The fountain in the eastern hemicycle of piazza del Popolo, under the slope of the Pincio: an armed Dea Roma flanked by seated figures of the Tiber and the Aniene, with the she-wolf and the twins at her feet.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza gives it as completed in 1823, by Valadier with Giovanni Ceccarini. The Sovrintendenza keeps a separate page for the fountain of the same name on the Campidoglio, in rione Campitelli, which is a different work; this record is the piazza del Popolo one.

places.name: Fontane sarcofago di piazza del Popolo
places.summary: Two Roman sarcophagi reused as fountains on the square, one set against Santa Maria del Popolo and the other against the barracks opposite.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza records them as part of Valadier's furnishing of the square between 1814 and 1828, replacing a drinking trough and a wash-house that until the eighteenth century had given the place a rural character. Valadier designed the sacristy and the whole convent flank of Santa Maria del Popolo, and the Giacomo Acqua barracks opposite, formerly the papal guards', as well. The strigilated sarcophagus by the church carries a portrait of a married couple in a clipeus and dates to the middle of the third century AD; the other, with a single togate male figure, to the last quarter of the same century.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria del Popolo
places.summary: The Augustinian basilica on the north side of piazza del Popolo, holding the Chigi, Cerasi and della Rovere chapels. No source states its visiting hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the church grew in the fifteenth century out of a small chapel built at the wish of Paschal II at the expense of the Roman people, from whom it takes its name. The Cappella Chigi, second on the left, was designed by Raphael for the banker Agostino Chigi from 1513 and finished between 1652 and 1656 with Bernini's intervention for Alexander VII Chigi; Raphael made the cartoons for the dome mosaics and the design for the pyramid tombs, executed by Lorenzetto, Raffaello da Montelupo and Bernini. The Cappella Cerasi in the left transept holds two Caravaggio canvases, the Crocifissione di San Pietro and the Conversione di San Paolo, both around 1601, commissioned in September 1600 by Tiberio Cerasi, treasurer of Clement VIII, with an Assunzione della Vergine by Annibale Carracci on the altar. The Cappella del Presepio, or della Rovere, is by Andrea Bregno, late fifteenth to early sixteenth century, frescoed by Pinturicchio and his workshop. A bull of Sixtus V made the basilica one of the seven churches pilgrims were to visit, in place of San Sebastiano fuori le Mura.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dei Miracoli
places.summary: The southern of the two churches that face the entrance of piazza del Popolo, standing between via del Corso and via di Ripetta.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that both churches were originally designed by Carlo Rainaldi and completed by Bernini with Carlo Fontana, and that they were conceived as symmetrical but built, for want of space, on different plans and with different domes, octagonal for Santa Maria dei Miracoli and dodecagonal for Santa Maria in Montesanto, so that from the square they read as identical through a purely optical effect.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Montesanto (Chiesa degli Artisti)
places.summary: The northern of the two churches facing the entrance of piazza del Popolo, standing between via del Corso and via del Babuino, and known as the Chiesa degli Artisti.
places.history: The basilica's own account dates the start of construction to 1662 under Alexander VII, on the site of a small church belonging to the Carmelites of the province of Monte Santo in Sicily; after an interruption the work resumed in 1673 under Carlo Fontana with Bernini supervising, and the interior decoration was finished in 1679. It became the Chiesa degli Artisti in 1953, when Monsignor Ennio Francia made it the seat of the Messa degli Artisti. Roma Capitale records the dodecagonal dome that distinguishes it from its twin.

places.name: Fontana in Piazza Nicosia
places.summary: One object with five addresses across four centuries. The Sovrintendenza records it as designed by Giacomo Della Porta in 1572 and originally set at the centre of piazza del Popolo, one of the public fountains built after the acquedotto Vergine was reactivated. it.wikipedia calls it the Fontana del Trullo, from piazza del Trullo, the older name of piazza del Popolo.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza records that a Falda engraving of 1665 shows the original form, an octagonal basin with two concentric round bowls on four dolphins. The fountain was dismantled around 1820 for Valadier's redesign of piazza del Popolo, rebuilt in the small square in front of San Pietro in Montorio on the Janiculum, removed again to municipal stores, and finally set in piazza Nicosia in 1950, in a new opening designed by Marcello Piacentini, 1881 to 1960, after the demolitions of 1936. The octagonal basin is the original element; a cipollino baluster carries a bowl decorated on the outside with Borghese heraldry. The travertine bollard fence was added in the restoration of 1998.

places.name: Chiesa e Convento della Trinità dei Monti
places.address: Piazza della Trinità dei Monti, Roma RM
places.summary: The church and convent at the head of the Spanish Steps, officiated also in French. Roma Capitale names it as one of the five French-speaking Catholic churches of Rome, with San Luigi dei Francesi, San Nicola dei Lorenesi, Sant'Ivo dei Bretoni and Santi Claudio e Andrea dei Borgognoni.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates the foundation to 1495. The convent's own site records that the domain was entrusted to the Communauté de l'Emmanuel by an accord of 25 July 2016 between the French State and the Holy See, that about twenty members of the community are in residence, and that guided visits are led by art historians licensed by the Regione Lazio. The complex also holds the Cappella di Mater Admirabilis, the Istituto Sacro Cuore and the casa per ferie San Giuseppe for pilgrims.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi Ambrogio e Carlo al Corso
places.summary: A minor basilica and rectory on via del Corso, which it.wikipedia gives as the national church of the Lombards resident in Rome.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that construction began in 1612, replacing a tenth-century building on the site, and that the church has been officiated by the Rosminians since 1906.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Antonio dei Portoghesi
places.summary: The national church of the Portuguese community in Rome, in rione Campo Marzio. It is also called Sant'Antonio in Campo Marzio, and the two names are the same building.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives the church as the national church of the Portuguese community in Rome, in rione Campo Marzio. The street it is addressed on, via dei Portoghesi, is one of the streets Roma Capitale names as the rione's boundary with Sant'Eustachio; the church itself stands inside Campo Marzio.

places.name: Chiesa di San Girolamo dei Croati
places.summary: The national church of the Croats in Rome, on via di Ripetta. It was formerly San Girolamo degli Illirici, or degli Schiavoni.
places.history: it.wikipedia records the older names, that the church is a rectory of San Lorenzo in Lucina and that it carries a cardinal title. Roma Capitale records that this church and San Rocco were spared when the quarter around the Mausoleum of Augustus was demolished from 1934.

places.name: Chiesa di San Rocco all'Augusteo
places.summary: A seventeenth-century church on piazza Augusto Imperatore, standing on the square laid out around the Mausoleum of Augustus.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives the church as seventeenth-century and in rione Campo Marzio. Roma Capitale records that it survived the demolitions of 1934, but was deprived of the hospital that adjoined it and of its bell tower.

places.name: Chiesa di Ognissanti (All Saints' Anglican Church)
places.summary: The Anglican church on via del Babuino, in the Church of England's Diocese in Europe. Its own site gives the services as Sundays Low Mass at 8.30 and Sung Mass with choir at 10.30, and Thursdays midweek Mass at 12.45, with worship in English.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church is also officiated by the Old Catholic community, and that it is one of the two Anglican churches of Rome, the other being San Paolo dentro le Mura, which stands in rione Castro Pretorio.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Atanasio dei Greci
places.summary: A rectory church on via del Babuino, officiated in the Byzantine rite. Sources give the street number as 149 and as 151. The two differ, so no number is given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the church in rione Campo Marzio, on via del Babuino, and records the Byzantine rite. Roma Capitale's Sovrintendenza records that the Babuino fountain was reassembled to the left of this church in 1957.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Nomi di Gesù e Maria
places.summary: A baroque church on via del Corso, in rione Campo Marzio, known in Rome simply as Gesù e Maria.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes it as a baroque church of Rome, on the central via del Corso, in rione Campo Marzio.

places.name: Chiesa di San Giacomo in Augusta
places.summary: The church attached to the hospital of the same name on via del Corso, also called San Giacomo degli Incurabili.
places.history: it.wikipedia records the church as annexed to the hospital of the same name, also known as San Giacomo degli Incurabili, and Wikidata gives the address as via del Corso 499.

places.name: Chiesa di Sant'Ivo dei Bretoni
places.summary: A church in vicolo della Campana, in French Église Saint-Yves-des-Bretons.
places.history: it.wikipedia places it in rione Campo Marzio, in vicolo della Campana, and counts it among the five French-speaking Catholic churches of Rome, with Trinità dei Monti, San Luigi dei Francesi, San Nicola dei Lorenesi and Santi Claudio e Andrea dei Borgognoni.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Portae Paradisi
places.summary: A church facing via di Ripetta, in rione Campo Marzio.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the church in rione Campo Marzio, facing onto via di Ripetta, and Wikidata gives the address as via di Ripetta 61.

places.name: Chiesa della Santissima Trinità degli Spagnoli
places.summary: A church at the via del Corso end of via dei Condotti, in rione Campo Marzio.
places.history: it.wikipedia places it in rione Campo Marzio, at the beginning of via dei Condotti, and Wikidata gives the address as via dei Condotti.

places.name: Chiesa di San Nicola dei Prefetti
places.summary: A church on via dei Prefetti, in rione Campo Marzio, commonly called San Nicola ai Prefetti.
places.history: it.wikipedia records both forms of the name and places the church in rione Campo Marzio, on via dei Prefetti.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Lucia della Tinta
places.address: Via di Monte Brianzo 61, Roma RM
places.summary: A small church on via di Monte Brianzo. Roma Capitale dates it to the tenth century and dedicates it to Lucy from 1394.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the church is named for the dyers of the ancient via Trinitatis, today via dei Condotti, which ran down to Ponte Sant'Angelo, and that the dedication to Lucy dates from 1394. Its account describes the façade and campanile, a single nave with three niches on each side and a polychrome coffered wooden ceiling.

places.name: Chiesa di San Gregorio dei Muratori
places.summary: An oratory at the end of an alley off via Leccosa, with a plan that runs across rather than along: the nave is wider than it is long, and the façade runs parallel to the nave, so the two doors open on the church's right side rather than at its end.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the oratory was built in 1527 by the Confraternita dei Muratori and dedicated to their patron, Gregory the Great; that it originally stood by the port of Ripetta; and that it is today enclosed inside a building of 1934. Inside are frescoes of the life of St Gregory, stucco putti and gilding, and the original terracotta floor.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Giorgio e Martiri inglesi
places.address: Via di San Sebastianello, Roma RM
places.summary: The English Catholic church on via di San Sebastianello, opened to the public on 5 November 1887 and served by an English women's congregation, the Poor Servants of the Mother of God, who occupy the attached convent.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church was built with a large donation from Prince Alessandro Torlonia and erected in memory of Lady Georgiana Fullerton, the congregation's founder, by her husband, and in memory also of their son William. The high altar canvas of St Gregory the Great is by A. Dies; the altar was Torlonia's gift and came from the demolished church of Santa Teresa alle Quattro Fontane, while the Madonna and Sacred Heart altars came from the demolished Sant'Elisabetta dei Fornari. The wall decoration is by Eugenio Cisterna.

places.name: Cappella di San Giovanni Battista de La Salle alla Piazza di Spagna
places.address: Via di San Sebastianello 1, Roma RM
places.summary: The chapel of the Collegio San Giuseppe Istituto De Mérode, dedicated to the founder of the Fratelli delle Scuole Cristiane.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the chapel in rione Campo Marzio, by via Alibert, with its postal address at via di San Sebastianello 1, and records the alternative name San Giovanni Battista de La Salle nel Collegio San Giuseppe Istituto De Mérode.

places.name: Rome Baptist Church
places.address: Piazza San Lorenzo in Lucina 35, Roma RM
places.summary: An English-language Protestant place of worship on piazza San Lorenzo in Lucina. it.wikipedia states that it stands in rione Campo Marzio; the basilica that gives the square its name is a separate building in rione Colonna.
places.history: No source states any history of the congregation.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Concezione in Campo Marzio
places.summary: The church on piazza Campo Marzio, with a rectory of the Syro-Antiochene rite. It is a different church from Santa Maria della Concezione dei Cappuccini, which stands in rione Ludovisi.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the church in rione Campo Marzio, on piazza Campo Marzio, and records the Syro-Antiochene rectory attached to it. The square it stands on is one of the streets Roma Capitale names as the rione's boundary; the church itself stands inside Campo Marzio.

places.name: Oratorio del Santissimo Sacramento di San Lorenzo in Lucina
places.summary: A deconsecrated oratory on via Belsiana, in rione Campo Marzio. It was built for a confraternity attached to the basilica of San Lorenzo in Lucina, which stands in rione Colonna.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that it was built in 1578 as the oratory of the house of the confraternity of the Santissimo Sacramento of San Lorenzo in Lucina; that it has a small entrance staircase and is decorated with large late-sixteenth-century oil-painted wooden panels; that between the late nineteenth and early twentieth century it hosted baroque music concerts; and that it was deconsecrated in 1970 and is now commercial premises, with the confraternity house behind it in civil use.

places.name: Pincio, Terrazza e Passeggiata
places.summary: The public promenade on the hill above piazza del Popolo, laid out with avenues wide enough for carriages and reached from the square by a monumental ramped access. it.wikipedia gives the hill as 61 m above sea level, north of the Quirinal and facing west over the Campo Marzio, ringed by the Aurelian Walls to north and east, and not one of the traditional seven hills.
places.history: The promenade was decided on in 1810, when the Napoleonic administration set out to create a public walk and Giuseppe Valadier presented a scheme linking piazza del Popolo to the Pincian hill. The central government sent the architect Louis Martin Berthault instead, who reworked it and proposed the elliptical form of the square. After 1814 the work returned to Valadier, who carried it through the Restoration to 1834. The promenade passed to the Municipio in 1848. Roma Capitale records that the access from piazza del Popolo climbs through three prospettive linked by small flights and by via Gabriele D'Annunzio: the first, of 1830, three niches with an antique Igea; the second, also of 1830, a relief of Fame crowning the Genii of the Arts and Commerce over a marble seat with two winged lions; and the third, a three-arched loggia carrying the Belvedere terrace, into which a nymphaeum was built in 1936 to a design by Raffaele De Vico, as a mostra of the Acqua Vergine, after an idea of Valadier's. The access off viale delle Magnolie is the one that has stayed strictly pedestrian.

places.name: Piazzale Napoleone I (the Pincio Belvedere)
places.summary: The terrace on the Pincio, carried on the three-arched loggia that closes the monumental access from piazza del Popolo.
places.history: Roma Capitale enumerates what is visible from the terrace: piazza del Popolo below, the dome of St Peter's on the horizon, Monte Mario to the right, the Quirinale to the left, and the equestrian monument to Garibaldi on the Janiculum in the distance.

places.name: Busti del Pincio
places.summary: The 229 commemorative busts of figures from Italian history set along the avenues of the Pincio. Roma Capitale and it.wikipedia both give the count as 229.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the busts were placed from 1849, and the Sovrintendenza's account of the promenade records that the first fifty busts of illustrious men were placed in 1849 at the commission of the republican government. it.wikipedia describes them as beginning as ordinary garden decoration and becoming small monuments to artists, writers and scientists, with a choice of subjects that is at once decorative, pedagogic and celebratory and tied to Risorgimento patriotic values.

places.name: Idrocronometro del Pincio
places.summary: The water clock on viale dell'Orologio, standing at the centre of a small lake inside an iron railing.
places.history: Roma Capitale writes that the mechanism is generally attributed to the Dominican father Giovanni Battista Embriaco, and keeps that hedge; this record keeps it too. The same source records that the hydrochronometer was placed in its present position in 1873.

places.name: Casina Valadier
places.summary: The neoclassical pavilion on the Pincio, a cubic block with an exedra and an Ionic colonnade, built to Valadier's design between 1816 and 1837 on the ancient Collis Hortulorum. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the building reworked the earlier Casino del Cardinale Della Rota, itself raised over a Roman cistern, and that the interiors were decorated in Pompeian style. It was used from the start as a bistro-style meeting place; it was closed and used as a garden store under Pius IX, with the cruciform attic given over to military quarters; it became a fashionable café for intellectuals after the First World War; German and then British officers used it as an officers' club during the Second; and it was restored in the early 2000s.

places.name: Villa Medici, Accademia di Francia a Roma
places.address: Viale della Trinità dei Monti 1, Roma RM
places.summary: The villa on the Pincian hill, seat of the French Academy in Rome, with a plain outer façade against an ornate inner one and gardens open to visitors. Roma Capitale gives the hours as open 9.30 to 19.00, last admission 18.30, closed Tuesday.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the present building is of the mid-sixteenth century, designed by Giovanni Lippi, called Nanni di Baccio Bigio, for Cardinal Giovanni Ricci da Montepulciano, who had bought the Casina Crescenzi on the collis hortulorum in 1564, with irrigation work by Camillo Agrippa. Cardinal Ferdinando de' Medici bought it in 1576 to house his art collection and in 1580 enclosed the villa between the Aurelian Walls and via Pinciana by buying Giulio Bosco's vineyard, creating the long north-south axis to the Parnaso. The inner façade carries garlands, masks, statues and antique reliefs and opens on a loggia over the gardens; the rectangular garden is divided into sixteen square beds, and the green estate covers over 7 hectares and largely keeps its sixteenth-century form. The Académie itself was founded in 1666 by Colbert, with Bernini, for the winners of the Prix de Rome, and has had its seat here since the early nineteenth century. The library, created in 1803 by Joseph-Benoît Suvée, director from 1795 to 1807, holds about 37,000 volumes, and the collections include portraits of 460 fellows from 1798 to 1936.

places.name: Monumento ai fratelli Cairoli
places.summary: A bronze monument on the Pincio to the brothers Enrico and Giovanni Cairoli.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the monument was raised in 1883 to the two Garibaldini, who were killed in 1867 at Villa Glori.

places.name: Monumento a Enrico Toti
places.summary: A monument to Enrico Toti on the Pincio.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the monument to Enrico Toti was raised in 1922.

places.name: Statue dei viali del Pincio
places.summary: The antique and nineteenth-century sculpture set along the avenues of the Pincio, which Roma Capitale enumerates as a single series.
places.history: Roma Capitale lists a small Raffaello Sanzio of 1838; a round fountain with Moses saved from the Nile, placed in 1868; the bust of Valadier closing viale del Belvedere; an Esculapio with a fifth-century body and a probably fourth-century head; and a Cibele of Antonine date which, with a Polimnia and an Abbondanza now standing in front of Villa Medici's entrance, was kept in the Palazzo dei Conservatori on the Campidoglio and moved to the Pincio in 1846.

places.name: Fontana della Vasca del Pincio
places.summary: The cup-shaped fountain on the panoramic front of the Pincio, facing Villa Medici.
places.history: Roma Capitale calls it the fontana a tazza known as the Vasca del Pincio and places it on the panoramic front of the promenade, facing Villa Medici.

places.name: Convento di Santa Rita al Pincio
places.summary: A convent on the Pincio, named by Roma Capitale in its walk-through of the hill, with a fountain adjoining it.
places.history: Roma Capitale describes the adjoining fountain as built from an antique oval basin of red granite of the second or third century, with a lion's head spout, set in a circular bowl.

places.name: Palazzo Borghese
places.address: Largo della Fontanella di Borghese, Roma RM
places.summary: The Borghese family palace, known in Rome as il cembalo for the shape of its plan. Roma Capitale records that the main façade opens on largo della Fontanella di Borghese while the building fills an irregular block between via di Ripetta, via dell'Arancio, via di Monte d'Oro, via della Fontanella di Borghese, via Borghese and piazza Borghese.
places.history: Roma Capitale dates the beginning to 1560, when Monsignor Tommaso del Giglio commissioned a palazzetto from Vignola; Martino Longhi il Vecchio completed and enlarged it for the Spanish cardinal Pedro Deza; and Cardinal Camillo Borghese, shortly to be Paul V, bought it in 1596, after which work continued under Flaminio Ponzio, then Carlo Maderno, Giovanni Vasanzio and, after 1670, Carlo Rainaldi. The monumental courtyard carries a double order of 96 Doric and Ionic columns, closed at the end by the nymphaeum known as the Bagno di Venere. Much of what hangs in the Galleria Borghese came from this palace; the Galleria itself is outside the rione.

places.name: Palazzo Ruspoli
places.summary: A palace with fronts on via del Corso and largo Goldoni, today the seat of the Fondazione Memmo, which mounts exhibitions in it. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the palace was built in the mid-sixteenth century by the Jacobilli, who ran out of money and sold it in 1583 to the Florentine Rucellai; they had Bartolomeo Ammannati, 1511 to 1592, finish it, giving it the via del Corso façade and a loggia over the garden whose gallery Jacopo Zucchi frescoed. The Caetani bought it in 1629 and had Bartolomeo Breccioli alter the largo Goldoni façade in 1630. Around 1640 Martino Longhi il Giovane, 1602 to 1656, built the staircase of over a hundred steps and the belvedere tower. It passed to the Ruspoli in 1776, who still own part of it. Handel composed La Resurrezione here as the Ruspoli princes' maestro di cappella, and Hortense de Beauharnais, former queen of Holland, stayed here with her two sons, one of whom became Napoleon III. In 1812 the ground-floor apartment housed the Caffè di Bagnoli, known as the Caffè Nuovo.

places.name: Palazzo Firenze
places.summary: The palace on piazza di Firenze, today the seat of the Società Dante Alighieri and of the Italian National Commission for UNESCO.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the palace belonged to the del Monte family and then to the Medici of Florence, from whom it takes its name; that it was formerly the Ministry of Grace and Justice; and that the Società Dante Alighieri has been there since 1926 and the Italian National Commission for UNESCO since 1950.

places.name: Palazzo Núñez-Torlonia
places.address: Via Bocca di Leone 79, Roma RM
places.summary: A palace filling the block between via dei Condotti, via Bocca di Leone and via Borgognona.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the palace in rione Campo Marzio between those three streets, and Wikidata gives the address as via Bocca di Leone 79.

places.name: Palazzetto Zuccari (Bibliotheca Hertziana)
places.summary: The house Federico Zuccari built at the top of via Gregoriana, known in Rome as the casa dei mostri for the door and window surrounds on that front. It houses the Bibliotheca Hertziana, the Max Planck Society's art-history research institute.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Zuccari built the palazzetto at the top of the street, that the monstrous surrounds gave it its nickname, and that after a long restoration in the early 2000s it houses the Bibliotheca Hertziana, an institute of the Max Planck Society dedicated to the history of art.

places.name: Palazzi dell'INPS a Piazza Augusto Imperatore
places.summary: The three buildings that close the north, east and south sides of piazza Augusto Imperatore around the Mausoleum of Augustus.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives the design to Vittorio Ballio Morpurgo, in rationalist style, laid out around the mausoleum with the Ara Pacis museum on the west side. Roma Capitale records that the square was closed on three sides by the three new INPS palaces, enriched with colonnades, bas-reliefs and mosaics.

places.name: Palazzo dell'ex Unione Militare
places.summary: An eclectic building of 1901 at the corner of via del Corso and via Tomacelli, restructured between 2008 and 2013.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the building at the corner of via del Corso and via Tomacelli in rione Campo Marzio, dates it to 1901 and records that it was restructured to a design by Massimiliano and Doriana Fuksas between 2008 and 2013.

places.name: Palazzo Rondinini
places.summary: An eighteenth-century palace on via del Corso, built for a collector and finished in 1764.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the palace was built for the Marchese Giuseppe Rondinini, a collector from Faenza, by enlarging a building that had belonged to the Cavalier d'Arpino. Gabriele Valvassori, the Doria Pamphilj family architect, did much of the exterior, and Alessandro Dori the via del Corso façade, the courtyard and the interiors. Four years of work were finished in 1764, when the collection moved in.

places.name: Palazzo Nainer
places.summary: A long-fronted palace on via del Babuino adjoining Santa Maria in Montesanto, built between 1818 and 1821 as part of Valadier's new scheme for piazza del Popolo and the Tridente. Part of it is now the Hotel Palazzo Nainer and the rest private flats.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that it was built over a former Augustinian monastery; that the long façade is in three parts, the central one in three orders articulated by pilasters, with a rusticated cornice separating the upper order and a balustraded terrace along the whole central section; that the Marchese Giampietro Campana bought it in the mid-nineteenth century and kept and showed part of his collection here; and that it was raised by a storey in 1872 during the works that followed Rome becoming capital.

places.name: Palazzo Aragona Gonzaga
places.summary: A sixteenth-century palace on via della Scrofa, also called Palazzo Balami Galitzin, Negroni or Mancini.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes it as late Renaissance, given a more baroque cast by a mid-eighteenth-century restoration, adjacent to the site of the Collegio Clementino, and records it as the residence of Cardinal Scipione Gonzaga. The via della Scrofa front carries plaques for St Aloysius Gonzaga and for Torquato Tasso.

places.name: Palazzo Capilupi
places.summary: A palace on via dei Prefetti, also called Palazzo Valdina Cremona, bounded by vicolo Rosini to the east and vicolo Valdina to the south.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives the address, the alternative name and the bounding alleys, and states outright that the building is in Municipio I, Rione IV Campo Marzio.

places.name: Palazzo Incontro
places.summary: A palace on via dei Prefetti built in the second half of the eighteenth century, in 1765, by the architect Giovanni Paolo Burij.
places.history: it.wikipedia records it as owned by the Provincia di Roma, which restored it between 2004 and 2007.

places.name: Palazzo Della Porta Negroni Caffarelli
places.summary: A palace on via dei Condotti, named at length to distinguish it from the family's other Roman houses.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the compound name separates it from Palazzo Caffarelli al Campidoglio, in rione Campitelli, from Palazzo Vidoni Caffarelli, and from Palazzo Aragona Gonzaga Negroni Galitzin, which stands on via della Scrofa in this rione.

places.name: Palazzo Corrodi
places.address: Lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, Roma RM
places.summary: A large building of the early 1900s that occupies a whole block between lungotevere Arnaldo da Brescia, via Luisa di Savoia, via Maria Adelaide and via Maria Cristina.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes it as an ample property of the beginning of the twentieth century occupying an entire block, and records that all four of the streets around it were instituted in 1904.

places.name: Palazzo Cardelli
places.summary: A palace on piazza Cardelli whose construction Roma Capitale dates from 1592, by Francesco da Volterra.
places.history: Roma Capitale describes two courtyards, the main one holding the stables and the second a well of the acqua vergine; an entrance hall with stuccoes and niches; coffered ceilings and tempera painting by Francesco Allegrini; and a roof garden with a stucco Apollo by Naldini. The Domus Magna façade is given to Francesco Capriani da Volterra and then Gaspare Guerra, and the rear of the building and the staircase to Francesco Peparelli, between 1630 and 1639.

places.name: Via del Babuino
places.summary: The eastern arm of the Tridente, running from piazza del Popolo to piazza di Spagna. it.wikipedia dates its opening to 1523 to 1527, under Clement VII, as the third of the three streets.
places.history: The street was formerly via Clementina, opened by Clement VII, and the Sovrintendenza records that it was renamed after the Babuino, the reclining Silenus fountain set against a palazzetto on it. All Saints', Sant'Atanasio dei Greci, Palazzo Nainer and the Museo Atelier Canova-Tadolini all stand on it.

places.name: Via di Ripetta
places.summary: The western arm of the Tridente, running from piazza del Popolo towards the river front and the Augustan monuments. it.wikipedia records that it was traced in 1518 under Leo X and was called via Leonina.
places.history: The street is named for the Porto di Ripetta, the river landing that stood in front of San Girolamo dei Croati and was demolished at the end of the nineteenth century. The Ara Pacis was reassembled in 1938 in a pavilion built on this street, and the Accademia di Belle Arti's historic seat stands at number 222.

places.name: Via dei Condotti
places.summary: The street that links via del Corso to piazza di Spagna.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that this was the ancient via Trinitatis, named for the dyers who worked along it and running down to Ponte Sant'Angelo; the church of Santa Lucia della Tinta takes its name from the same trade. The Antico Caffè Greco is at number 86, Palazzo Magistrale at 68, Palazzo Della Porta Negroni Caffarelli at 61 and the church of the Santissima Trinità degli Spagnoli at 41.

places.name: Via Gregoriana
places.summary: The street opened to link Trinità dei Monti to the city below, with the Palazzetto Zuccari and its monstrous door and window surrounds at its head.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the street was opened by Gregory XIII for the Jubilee of 1575, replacing Domenico Fontana's staircase, to link Trinità dei Monti to the city below.

places.name: Via Borgognona
places.summary: One of the Tridente cross-streets between piazza di Spagna and via del Corso.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that it runs parallel between via dei Condotti to the north and via Frattina to the south. Palazzo Núñez-Torlonia and Palazzo di Spagna both extend onto it.

places.name: Lungotevere in Augusta
places.summary: The river front of the rione, running along the embankment below piazza Augusto Imperatore.
places.history: it.wikipedia's history of the rione records the Tiber floods and the muraglioni built after 1870 to stop them, and that the new lungotevere in Augusta and lungotevere Marzio were named as the embankment was laid out. Roma Capitale names lungotevere in Augusta among the streets that form the rione's boundary.

places.name: Piazza Borghese
places.summary: The square on the flank of Palazzo Borghese, faced today by a building of the Sapienza architecture faculty.
places.history: Roma Capitale records Borghese settlement here from the sixteenth century, and the expansion under Paul V, 1605 to 1621, and Cardinal Scipione Borghese between via di Ripetta and San Girolamo degli Schiavoni. The square remained a private space attached to the palace until the nineteenth century, and was closed on the via di Ripetta side between 1923 and 1928 by the building that now houses the Sapienza architecture faculty.

places.name: Ponte Cavour
places.summary: A bridge of the rione. it.wikipedia records that it lies in two rioni, Campo Marzio and Prati, so the far bank is not Campo Marzio's.
places.history: it.wikipedia's history of the rione records that the bridge was built in 1902 and that the site of the Porto di Ripetta, the old river landing in front of San Girolamo dei Croati, was covered by it.

places.name: Il Babuino (Fontana del Babuino)
places.summary: The fountain that gave via del Babuino its name: an ancient grey granite basin under a life-size tufa Silenus reclining on rocks, set in a niche. Roma Capitale names it among the statue parlanti, with Pasquino, Marforio, Madama Lucrezia and Abate Luigi, on which Romans posted anonymous complaints.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza dates it to about 1576 and describes it as a semipubblica fountain, built at the expense of a private citizen, the Ferrara merchant Alessandro Grandi, but for public use, and set in a niche on his palazzetto. It explains the nickname by the figure's ugliness. It was moved left to number 49a in the rebuilding of 1738 by the Boncompagni-Ludovisi, and dismembered in 1877 for sewer works, the Silenus going to the Boncompagni courtyard and the basin to via Flaminia. It was reassembled in 1957 on the opposite side of the street from its original position, to the left of Sant'Atanasio dei Greci. The Silenus is antique, its head does not belong to it, and it has also been identified with the Sabine god Sanco Fidio Semicapro. The street had been via Clementina, opened by Clement VII, before it was renamed after the statue. Of the talking statues, Marforio stands in rione Campitelli and Pasquino in rione Parione.

places.name: Accademia di Belle Arti di Roma, sede storica
places.summary: The historic seat of Rome's fine arts academy, on via di Ripetta. The Academy's own contacts page gives the address and the opening as 07.30 to 19.15, Monday to Saturday. A second Roman site, the succursale at via del Corso 476, is also inside the rione.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the Academy belongs to the AFAM sector of higher education under Legge 508/1999.

places.name: Casa di Goethe
places.summary: The apartment on via del Corso where Goethe lived between 1786 and 1788, opened as a museum in 1997. Roma Capitale gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00, closed Monday, with last admission half an hour before closing.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Goethe shared the apartment with the painters Tischbein, Johann Georg Schütz and Friedrich Bury; that the collection covers German artists from the poet's Roman circle alongside contemporary Italian and German work, with a permanent display called Goethe in Italia; and that it holds Andy Warhol's 1982 portrait of Goethe, made after Tischbein. There are two libraries, that of the Deutscher Künstlerverein and a reference library of about 8,500 volumes.

places.name: Museo Atelier Canova-Tadolini
places.summary: A sculptor's studio kept as a museum with a café and restaurant inside it, at the corner of via del Babuino and via dei Greci. Its own site gives the bar and caffetteria as open daily 08.00 to 24.00 and the restaurant daily 12.00 to 23.00.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that in January 1818 Antonio Canova signed to guarantee the lease of his studio di uso di cultura in favour of his pupil Adamo Tadolini, with leave to reproduce some of his works, and that Canova had himself worked in the rooms. The atelier remained Tadolini family property from 1818 until the late 1960s, through four generations, Adamo, Giulio, Scipione and Enrico, who made over 500 works in it. It was later bought by the Galleria Antiquaria Benucci and reopened to the public in 2003 as a restaurant and café inside a museum. About 400 works are shown: sketches, preparatory models, marble and bronze sculpture, anatomical studies, tools and documents.

places.name: Antico Caffè Greco
places.summary: The coffee house at via dei Condotti 86. it.wikipedia records that it was temporarily closed during 2025 by the Ospedale Israelitico di Roma and that a reopening was reported in May 2026, and the business's own site currently carries a campaign about the future of the premises. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records the founding in 1760 by Nicola di Madalena, a Levantine coffee-seller, from whom the name comes, and counts over 300 works on the walls, with the Sala Omnibus holding medallions, miniatures and plaster plaques recording Bizet, Baudelaire, Byron, D'Annunzio, Goethe, Joyce, Leopardi, Nietzsche, Silvio Pellico, Buffalo Bill and Sitting Bull. Roma Capitale also lists it among the city's historic shops. it.wikipedia records that the Gruppo dei Romanisti meets here on the first Wednesday of every month and has published the Strenna dei Romanisti each year on 21 April, the Natale di Roma, since 1940, and that the café belongs to Locali storici d'Italia, a private association.

places.name: Il Vero Alfredo
places.summary: A restaurant on piazza Augusto Imperatore, with about 450 photographs on its walls. Roma Capitale lists it among the city's historic shops and gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday 12.30 to 15.30 and 19.30 to 23.30, closed Monday lunchtime.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the business began in 1908 in a small restaurant in Piazza Rosa, on the site later occupied by the Galleria Alberto Sordi, when Alfredo Di Lelio made fettuccine of semolino with butter and parmesan for his wife Ines after childbirth; that it moved to via della Scrofa in 1914; and that Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks, honeymooning in Rome, gave him two gold serving pieces. The via della Scrofa premises were given up around the Second World War, and his son Armando, Alfredo II, restarted afterwards on piazza Augusto Imperatore. Roma Capitale names Alfredo III alongside Ines Di Lelio in the family that runs it.

places.name: Grand Hotel Plaza
places.summary: A hotel on via del Corso, in the Tridente. Roma Capitale writes that it began as an inn in the last decade of papal Rome and became a meeting point for nobles, artists and politicians.
places.history: Roma Capitale's feature on the city's historic hotels explains that Federalberghi Roma gathered hotels founded before 1950 into a Comitato Alberghi Storici with over forty members, about half of them four- or five-star. That is a fact about the committee rather than about this hotel, and no source states how long the business has traded.

entries.name: Scalinata di Trinità dei Monti
entries.note: Built 1723 to 1726 to Francesco De Sanctis' design, finished under Benedict XIII, restored from October 2015 and walkable again from 23 September 2016.

entries.name: Piazza del Popolo
entries.note: The point where via del Babuino, via di Ripetta and via del Corso meet, given its ellipse by Valadier from 1811 and finished in 1828.

entries.name: Ara Pacis Augustae
entries.note: The altar voted by the Senate in 13 BC and inaugurated in 9 BC, buried by Tiber silt and reassembled in the summer of 1938 under Giuseppe Moretti.

entries.name: Museo dell'Ara Pacis
entries.note: Roma Capitale gives the museum as open daily 9.30 to 19.30, with 9.30 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December and last admission an hour before closing.

entries.name: Mausoleo di Augusto
entries.note: Closed since 6 June 2022 while work on piazza Augusto Imperatore goes forward, so plan to see the 87 m drum from the square rather than inside.

entries.name: Pincio, Terrazza e Passeggiata
entries.note: The promenade decided on in 1810 and carried through by Valadier to 1834, climbing from piazza del Popolo by three prospettive to the Belvedere loggia.

entries.name: Piazzale Napoleone I
entries.note: Roma Capitale lists the sightlines: piazza del Popolo below, St Peter's dome on the horizon, Monte Mario right, the Quirinale left, Garibaldi on the Janiculum.

entries.name: Villa Medici
entries.note: Seat of the Académie founded in 1666 by Colbert; gardens of over 7 hectares in sixteen square beds. Open 9.30 to 19.00, last admission 18.30, closed Tuesday.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria del Popolo
entries.note: The Chigi chapel designed by Raphael from 1513 and the Cerasi chapel with two Caravaggio canvases of about 1601. No source states its visiting hours.

entries.name: Fontana in Piazza Nicosia
entries.note: Della Porta's fountain of 1572, made for piazza del Popolo, rebuilt on the Janiculum, stored, and finally set in piazza Nicosia in 1950.

entries.name: Casa di Goethe
entries.note: The apartment where Goethe lived from 1786 to 1788, a museum since 1997; Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00, last admission half an hour before closing.

entries.name: Babingtons
entries.note: A tea room on piazza di Spagna founded in 1893 by Anna Maria Babington and Isabel Cargill, open Monday to Sunday 10.00 to 21.15.

entries.name: Il Vero Alfredo
entries.note: Fettuccine with butter and parmesan, made first in 1908 by Alfredo Di Lelio; Tuesday to Sunday 12.30 to 15.30 and 19.30 to 23.30, closed Monday lunchtime.

entries.name: Grand Hotel Plaza
entries.note: A hotel on via del Corso which Roma Capitale writes began as an inn in the last decade of papal Rome.
